name: Bahamas Creole English
confidence_why: The only first-hand description, Childs & Wolfram 2004, says Bahamian prosody has never been studied in detail and offers just two words (Cherokée, moráy) stressed off the initial syllable, while Hackert 2013's line that word stress is "generally on the first syllable" is a one-sentence paraphrase of that same passage, so no placement or type of stress can be stated for Bahamian Creole with any confidence.

Schneider, Kate Burridge, Bernd Kortmann, Rajend Mesthrie & Clive Upton (eds.), A handbook of varieties of English, vol. 1: Phonology, 435-449. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. (Reprinted 2008 in Schneider (ed.), Varieties of English 2: The Americas and the Caribbean, 239-255, doi:10.1515/9783110208405.1.239.) Secondary gloss: Hackert, Stephanie. 2013. Bahamian Creole. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), The survey of pidgin and creole languages, vol. 1, 127-138. Oxford: OUP; APiCS Online survey chapter 12, sec. 4 Phonology.
catalog_locator: Childs & Wolfram 2004, sec. 3.3 'Prosodic features', pp. 447-448: the 'no detailed research' sentence opens the section on p. 447; the primary-stress sentence and 'still awaits extensive, detailed study' close it on p. 448. Hackert 2013, APiCS Online survey ch. 12, sec. 4 'Phonology', last paragraph.
catalog_quote: There have been few comprehensive studies of prosody in the Caribbean and North American islands and no detailed research on these features in Bahamian English. Wells (1982) describes the general prosodic characteristics of speech as sounding more syllable-timed than stress-timed. ... One of the most recognizable features of Bahamian English is the relative lack of reduction of vowels in unstressed syllables as in most varieties of American English. This trait contributes to the perception of Bahamian English as being stress-timed rather than syllable- timed. ... In addition, there also are some stress differences in the assignment of primary stress. For example, in some cases primary stress may occur on non-initial syllables rather than the first syllable, as in Cherokée for Cherokee or moráy for moray. Bahamian English still awaits extensive, detailed study of prosodic features, though it is clearly an essential part of the phonetic configuration of white and black Bahamian varieties.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-read the named on-disk file (2.79 MB HTML text of Handbook of Varieties of English vol. 1; the Bahamian chapter 'Bahamian English: phonology, Becky Childs and Walt Wolfram' begins at p. 435). Section 3.3 'Prosodic features' is present exactly as excerpted in the '447' page header precedes 3.2.7 Sibilants and 3.3, and the '448 Becky Childs and Walt Wolfram' header falls mid-sentence in the intonation remark, so the vowel-reduction sentence is p. 447 and the primary-stress sentence ('In addition, there also are some stress differences in the assignment of primary stress. For example, in some cases primary stress may occur on non-initial syllables rather than the first syllable, as in Chero…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positive rule is stated by the primary description. Word stress is lexical, inherited from the English lexifier; the only descriptive content is that some words carry primary stress on a non-initial syllable where other Englishes have initial stress (Cherokée, moráy), that unstressed vowels are little reduced, and that rhythm tends toward syllable timing. The open secondary sketch (Hackert 2013, APiCS survey ch. 12, sec. 4) glosses these same pages as 'Word stress is generally on the first syllable' — a paraphrase not supported word-for-word by the pages it cites, so it is recorded as a gloss, not as the deciding statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Bahamian. Schneider's synopsis (same volume, p. 1088) only remarks in general that American English preserves secondary stress more strongly than British-based varieties.
new_statements.exceptions: Cherokée for Cherokee, moráy for moray (non-initial primary stress). Schneider's synopsis (pp. 1087-1088) adds that unstressed word-initial syllables are variably omitted in Bahamian ('bout, 'cept) and lists Bahamian among varieties reported as relatively syllable-timed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, impressionistic, no instrumental study ('no detailed research on these features'); covers both Afro-Bahamian (creole) and Anglo-Bahamian (white) speech without distinguishing them for stress; Hackert 2013 reports the same for Bahamian Creole. Intonation remarks (high-rising terminals on affirmatives, wide pitch range) are sentence-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Childs & Wolfram 2004 is titled 'Bahamian English' and covers both Afro-Bahamian (basilectal creole, = baha1260) and Anglo-Bahamian (white Bahamian) speech, treating stress for both together; Hackert 2013 ('Bahamian Creole', APiCS ch. 12) is explicitly baha1260 and reports the same. No separate glottocode exists for Anglo-Bahamian English; Turks and Caicos speech is turk1310 and not covered here.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 Prosodic features (pp. 447-448): 'no detailed research on these features in Bahamian English'; speech sounds more syllable-timed than stress-timed (after Wells 1982) but not absolutely; 'relative lack of reduction of vowels in unstressed syllables'; 'some stress differences in the assignment of primary stress.. in some cases primary stress may occur on non-initial syllables rather than the first syllable, as in Cherokée for Cherokee or moráy for moray'; high-rising terminal intonation on affirmatives; 'still awaits extensive, detailed study of prosodic features'.

sources.note: Sec. 4 Phonology, last paragraph: 'As for prosody, Bahamian Creole has been described as more syllable-timed than British or American varieties of English, but syllable timing is not absolute. Word stress is generally on the first syllable. Noteworthy intonation patterns include the high rising terminal contours of affirmative sentences and a wider pitch range.. (Childs & Wolfram 2004: 447-448).' Second-hand gloss of Childs & Wolfram; Google Books snippet of the print volume (id NZkeAAAAQBAJ) shows the same sentence near p. 129.

sources.note: Sec. 8 Prosodic features (pp. 1087-1088): unstressed word-initial syllables omitted ('bout, 'cept) 'variably . BahE'; stress shift from first to a later syllable (indi'cate, holi'day) reported for T&TC, TobC and sometimes JamE/C etc. but Bahamian not named for it; 'a tendency toward a relatively syllable-timed rather than a stress-timed rhythm is reported.. quite strongly (TobC, T&TC, Baj, JamC, BahE)'. Region-level survey, second-hand.
